title: The First Light
dateline: The research base. The evening of the first light.
mood: The frame in the lab finally holds its light, and nobody wants to go to bed.

hero.alt: A framed photograph stands on a bright lab bench: two smiling scientists in white coats hold a small pink-haired girl up between them, while the lab behind is soft with light.

segs.t: Chang’e laid a spoon beside the fourth plate and set it straight.
Nobody would use it. The chair in front of it faced the door, and it had been empty for nine days. Every night since Sis left, her mother had set the plate anyway.
Mr. Bunny hung over the table with a 9 on his screen. Each morning he showed a new number.
“Nine days,” said Chang’e.
“Eight and a half,” said her father, over his soup. “She left at dawn.”
Chang’e stared at him.
“He counts too,” said her mother. “He just won’t say so.”
“I’m rounding up,” said Chang’e.

No word had come from Sis. Nobody had expected any, because her comm had been off since the road outside the gate. The soldier who had the gate now walked no rounds. At midnight Chang’e listened for one anyway.
“Two hundred and forty-one last night,” said her mother. She tapped her pencil on the table. “Tonight, I think.”
Chang’e put down her spoon. “Sis isn’t back.”
“No.”
“I told her to be back for it.”
“Then we show her again when she is.” Her mother pointed the pencil at her. “If it only works once, it doesn’t work.”
Chang’e looked for a hole in that and could not find one.
The frame stood at the back of the lab, beside the test ring. In the wire cage at its chest the piece lay dark. The fourth stool stood beside it, empty.
Her mother sat with her notebook on her knee. Her father stood with his hands in his pockets.
Chang’e pressed her palm to the copper plate in the frame’s hand.
She thought of the gate bolt banging. Boots in the yard. Sis in the lab door, back for it, as she had promised.
The light woke in the cage. It did not shake.
“One,” said her mother. “Two.”
Come home for this,
thought Chang’e. She kept her hand flat.
Come home.
At a hundred, her mother’s voice went up a little. At two hundred and six she glanced at the cage and went on. Two hundred and forty-one. Three hundred.
The pencil went down. Her mother had stopped counting.
The frame began to hum. The sound came up through the steel tubes and into Chang’e’s palm. It had never done that before.
Her father took both hands out of his pockets.
“That’s it,” said her mother. Her voice cracked in the middle. “That’s the first light.”
“It isn’t shaking,” said Chang’e.
“No. It’s holding.”
Her mother laughed and caught her under the arms. Her father took her other side. Between them they lifted her up, the way they held her in the photograph on the bench.
Her hand came off the plate. In the cage the light sank slowly, as it always did when she let go.
Her father nearly smiled. “Your hand did that,” he said.
Chang’e held the hand up in front of her face and looked at it. Then she held it out so they could both see.
“Again,” she said. “Tomorrow.”
“Tomorrow,” said her mother. “And the day after. And then for Lesley.”
The laugh had carried down the corridor. Three of the night shift stood in the lab door. One was the researcher who had sent Chang’e off the big bench.
“Who did that?” he asked.
Her mother pointed at Chang’e.
He looked from her to the cage. “The big bench is yours,” he said, and took the others back to work.
Afterward her mother took three caramel puddings from the cold box under the bench. She tapped her cup against Chang’e’s. Her father held his out too, without being asked.
“Will Sis be the first to wear it?” asked Chang’e.
Her mother looked across at her father. He nodded, once.
Chang’e took a fourth cup from the cold box. She wrote SIS across its lid in pencil and put it back at the front, where nobody could miss it.
She climbed up to the console and opened her design log.
Lesley, it held! You missed it. Come home.
She saved it for Sis to read at the door.
Past midnight the lab was still lit. Nobody wanted to go to bed.
The page pinned to the frame’s foot still said who it was for.
For whoever has to stand in front.
Under it, in her quick hand, her mother wrote two more words:
First light.
Then she went back to her notebook, writing up the night. Her father had the frame’s wrist open and was tightening something that did not need it.
Far off, sirens had started at the city’s edge. They went there most weeks. Her father glanced at the window, then went back to the wrist.
At the end of the bench, beside the photograph, Chang’e was giving Mr. Bunny a new face for when Sis came home. It had one round eye and one teal one, and the teal one winked.
Across the lab, her mother looked over and laughed until she had to wipe her glasses.
“Bed,” she said, still laughing.
“After his face. The wink’s too slow.”
Chang’e switched him off and opened his casing. His screen went dark.
Then the alarm went, and every lamp in the lab turned red.

Through the window, half the city was burning. Small flying craft shaped like cars swept low over the base’s grounds. One fired into the storehouse across the yard, and its roof went up in a sheet of flame.
Chang’e ran to the lab door and opened it. The corridor flashed red. Researchers ran past with their arms full.
She made her face serious, the way Sis’s face was at the gate.

media.alt: From high above, a city by the water burns at night while flying craft sweep low over it; then a corridor flashes red and a figure hurries past; then a door slides open on Chang'e's face, lit red, serious behind her round glasses.

segs.t: Behind her, Mr. Bunny lay dark on the bench beside the photograph, his casing open. She turned back for him.
“Leave him,” said her father.
“I can close him up.”
“Leave him.” He put a hand on her shoulder. “Stay close, Chang’e.”
His voice was calm. It was always calm.
Her mother crouched, did up the top button of Chang’e’s coat, the one Chang’e always forgot, and took her hand.

Outside, smoke drifted across the stars, and the air tasted of burning plastic. Her father’s arm went round her mother’s shoulders. Chang’e pressed against her mother’s side, held the hand tight and shut her eyes.
“The shelter,” said her father. “Fifty steps.”
They ran across the yard. Chang’e let the hand pull her.
As they ran, her mother put the radio from her coat to her mouth. “Lesley. Lesley, come in.”
The radio hissed.
“Lesley.”
Nothing.
She’s coming,
Chang’e thought, with her eyes shut.
She promised.
“Thirty,” said her father.
The ground jumped under her feet. Then again, closer.
“Twenty.”
Then he stopped counting.

media.alt: Chang'e's father runs with his arm round her mother's shoulders, Chang'e clinging to her mother's hand with her eyes shut, while behind them a giant black and gold Ender with long curved blades towers over the burning street, a pink glow at its chest.

segs.t: Chang’e opened her eyes.
A giant Ender was walking through the middle of the city. It stood hundreds of meters tall, black and gold, on tall thin legs. Huge curved blades hung from its arms. Smoke curled around its knees.
It did not hurry. It walked like a machine doing what it was told.
The head turned, and it looked down at the yard.
Its chest plates opened. Light gathered behind them, gold, then white.
Her parents stopped. Her father’s arm came away from her mother’s shoulders, and they turned to face it, with Chang’e between them.
Her mother let go of her hand. “Chang’e!”
Hands shoved her, one pair from each side, and she was out from between them.
She fell and rolled across the stones. When she looked up, she saw their backs.
Two white coats stood in front of her, between her and the light. They took a step toward it. They did not turn around.
Her own hand was reaching after them. She did not remember putting it out.
Then the light came down, and everything was white.
For a long time there was only ringing.
When she could see again, there was a crater. There was nothing in it.
She knelt at its edge in the ash, black with soot. Her legs would not move. Her glasses had slid down her nose, and she did not push them up.
Her mouth made the word
Mom
. No sound came with it.
A moment ago her mother’s hand had been in hers. She looked at her fingers.
I had my eyes shut,
she thought.
I let them pull me.
Nothing came around to the front.
The ground shook again, farther off. The giant was leaving.
Across the crater, something tall and gray stepped up to the rim. It turned toward her.
She did not move.
A shot cracked close by.
